title: Ministers insist kilt bond scheme 'not in doubt' as experts warn of budget black hole
excerpt: Finance experts told Holyrood's Finance Committee that the Scottish Government's £1.5bn bond programme will cost more than conventional borrowing and leave a future budget exposed yet ministers refuse to publish the calculations behind their value-for-money case.
content:
Ministers have vowed to push ahead with a £1.5 billion Scottish bond scheme despite stark warnings from finance experts that the "badly designed" plan leaves a future budget black hole.

Holyrood's Finance Committee was told the five-year borrowing drive will cost taxpayers more than traditional UK Government loans while failing to deliver any long-term financial benefits.

University of Stirling finance professor David McMillan warned MSPs that with no rollover arrangement or cash reserve in place, repaying the 10-to-15-year bonds will rip "a huge chunk of money" out of a future Scottish budget.

Auditor General Stephen Boyle also raised concerns over transparency after ministers refused to publish calculations backing up their value-for-money claims, citing commercial sensitivity.

Despite the backlash, Deputy First Minister Jenny Gilruth insisted the plans were "not in doubt" during Wednesday's portfolio questions, telling MSPs that ministers would remain "prudent" and assess market conditions before issuing the debt.

Ministers plan to sell £300 million of bonds a year for five years, with the £1.5bn raised to be used "exclusively for capital investment".

The bonds themselves could run for 10 or 15 years.

After the initial five issuances, the government will review whether to keep going or return to borrowing only from the National Loans Fund.

Bonds will, initially, cost more than the National Loans Fund. The government's case for paying the extra is that building a track record with investors, getting Scotland known in the markets, showing that it can manage debt reliably, will mean ministers can borrow more cheaply and flexibly in future.

John Swinney wants to spend the £1.5bn raised on infrastructure

At the committee, Prof McMillan said these long-term gains would never come about while the programme was limited to five years.

He told MSPs: "Why does Scotland want a bond programme that replicates essentially what it has through the National Loans Fund but at a higher cost? The only reason ultimately for doing that is because the long-term benefits, 25 years plus, would outweigh the current costs.

"The way the bond programme is structured, those 25-year-plus benefits are not going to ever arise because it's going to end in five years with no rollover."

He added: "I would not design a programme that looks like this. I would not design a programme that says, in five years' time, we will think about it, because investors are looking for permanence in the nature of the programme."

Prof McMillan was asked whether there were any safeguards to make sure future governments could afford the repayments.

He said: "Nothing that I've seen suggests that that is in place at the moment, so it's a case of we're going to issue these bonds now, let's say it's for 10 years, and in 10 years' time we're going to fully repay them and that full repayment will come from the budget that exists in that year."

He said that unless a rollover was agreed with the UK Government or a reserve was built up, "when it gets to the 10th year you're going to be taking a huge chunk of money out of that budget".

Mr Boyle told the committee: "If there are no rollover arrangements, this will have to be repaid at the end of the original term and that will have to be managed. I suppose what we've seen over recent years is an increasing complexity with the Scottish Government's budget arrangements, particularly up until now with budget reconciliations that add volatility that have to be accounted for. This would be another new complexity."

The Scottish Government has said that, in the right market conditions, bonds could offer better value than the National Loans Fund in net present value terms. It has refused to publish the calculations behind that claim on the grounds of commercial sensitivity.

Dr Ben Cormier, Senior Lecturer at the University of Strathclyde, said that argument did not stand up.

He said: "For me, not so much. It's also pretty straightforward to estimate these things. I think in the Financial Times, I saw an estimate that the bonds would be 30 basis points above UK gilts. If the FT can get an estimate, I'm not sure why we couldn't."

Mr Boyle said: "Transparency and openness is absolutely fundamental, bearing in mind after all this is public money, public debt and public money that will be used to repay the debt."

Lenaic Couderc, an assistant vice president with Moody's Ratings, told the committee that Scotland's credit rating, which matches the UK's, was "very much a rating based on the current set of circumstances". That includes Scotland's place in the UK and the likelihood of the UK Government stepping in if anything went wrong.

Dr Cormier said: "Fundamentally all the discussion of risk associated with Scottish bonds comes down to a constitutional question. If it were to ever go sideways, the UK Government would be there. So the risk to investors is essentially nil."

Asked whether markets were pricing in the SNP's position that Scotland would be independent by 2031, he said: "I think it's priced in, but they don't see a high likelihood of that happening."

Prof McMillan said that if ministers issued bonds of 40 or 50 years, the market would add "a bigger constitutional risk premium".

Scottish Tory MSP Craig Hoy pushed the government on the scheme (Image: PA)

On Wednesday afternoon, during portfolio questions, Scottish Tory finance spokesman Craig Hoy said the government's plans were in "serious doubt due to surging borrowing costs and fears about what might happen if ever, God forbid, Scotland became independent".

He said this was "an entirely unnecessary process" and that Ms Gilruth should stick with borrowing through the "tried and tested means of the National Loans Fund".

Ms Gilruth said: "I am always pleased to hear a mention of independence in this chamber coming from a Conservative MSP.

"But no, to answer the member's substantive point, the plans are not in doubt and we have been very clear that any decision around about the progress of the bonds programme will be subject to the necessary requirements looking at the market conditions at the time.

"You would expect the Government to be prudent on these matters and looking at the market conditions at the time would be a necessary requirement for us engaging on these matters."
